title: Kava Hangover: Why Kava Leaves You Groggy and How to Feel Better
excerpt: Does kava give you a hangover? How kava grogginess differs from an alcohol hangover, why tudei kava makes it worse, what helps, and signs that need a doctor.
metaDescription: Does kava give you a hangover? How kava grogginess differs from an alcohol hangover, why tudei kava is worse, what helps, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, kava can leave you feeling off the next morning, but a "kava hangover" is usually much milder than an alcohol hangover and it feels different. Most people describe it as grogginess: heavy limbs, slow thinking, low motivation, and a sleepy, "wrapped in cotton" feeling that lifts by late morning or midday. You don't usually get the pounding headache, the nausea, the thirst, and the anxious jittery feeling that a big night of drinking brings. The main things that make a kava hangover worse are drinking a lot of it, drinking the wrong kind (so-called "tudei" or "two-day" kava), drinking it on an empty stomach, and mixing it with alcohol.

**The quick rules:** Stick to noble kava from a seller who says which variety it is. Drink a moderate amount, eat something, and give yourself a full night's sleep. Don't mix kava with alcohol, because you get the alcohol hangover plus the kava grogginess on top, and the two together add up to more sedation than either alone. Don't drive the night of a session or the next morning if you still feel slow. Most kava grogginess clears with food, water, daylight, and time.

> **When to see a doctor.** This is not medical advice, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. A normal kava hangover is mild and fades within a day. **See a doctor promptly if** you notice yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes, dark urine, pale stools, pain under your right ribs, unusual tiredness that lasts for days, or nausea and loss of appetite that won't go away. These can be signs of liver trouble, which is rare with kava but has been reported. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US)** if someone who has used kava, especially together with alcohol or sedating medicine, is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is confused, or can't stay upright. Talk to your doctor before using kava at all if you have liver disease, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or take medicine for anxiety, sleep, pain, depression, or seizures.

## What Is a Kava Hangover?

Kava is a drink made from the ground root of *Piper methysticum*, a plant in the pepper family that has been used across the South Pacific for a very long time, in places like Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga, Samoa, and Hawaii. In the US it's sold in kava bars, as powdered root you mix with water, and as capsules, tinctures, and "shots."

The active compounds are called **kavalactones**. There are six main ones that make up most of the effect, and different kava varieties carry them in different proportions. That mix is a big part of why one kava leaves you calm and clear and another leaves you heavy and sluggish the next day.

A "kava hangover" is the name people give to the leftover effects the morning after a session. It isn't a medical term, and there isn't much formal research on it. What we have is a lot of consistent reports from regular kava drinkers plus some knowledge of how kavalactones work. Put together, the picture is fairly clear:

- **Grogginess and heaviness.** The most common complaint. You feel like you slept deeply but didn't fully wake up.
- **Slow thinking and low motivation.** Tasks feel harder to start. Some people call it "kava lag."
- **Lethargy that lifts with time.** It usually fades over the morning, sooner once you eat and move around.
- **Mild nausea or an unsettled stomach.** More common after a big session, kava on an empty stomach, or poor-quality or tudei kava.
- **Sometimes a mild headache or dry, tired eyes.** Usually far milder than an alcohol headache.

Things people generally *don't* report after a normal amount of kava: the intense thirst, the racing heart, the shakiness, and the next-day anxiety that often follow heavy drinking.

## Does Kava Give You a Hangover?

It can, but it depends heavily on how much you drink and what kind.

After a cup or two of good-quality noble kava, many people wake up feeling normal, or even rested. After a long session with many shells, or after strong tudei kava, a groggy morning is common. Think of it less like a hangover in the alcohol sense and more like the heavy feeling some people get after a strong sleep aid. The sedating effect simply hasn't fully worn off yet.

The amount matters more than people expect. Kava bars often serve many rounds over an evening, and it's easy to drink far more than you would at home. Concentrated extracts, "kava shots," and high-strength capsules can also deliver a lot of kavalactones quickly.

## Kava Grogginess vs Alcohol Hangover: How They Compare

The two feel different because they come from different causes. An alcohol hangover is a whole-body event. A kava hangover is mostly a leftover-sedation event.

| | Kava hangover | Alcohol hangover |
|---|---|---|
| Main feeling | Groggy, heavy, slow, sleepy | Headache, nausea, fatigue, "poisoned" feeling |
| Headache | Uncommon, usually mild | Common, often throbbing |
| Nausea | Sometimes, usually mild | Common, can include vomiting |
| Thirst and dehydration | Usually minor | Common, because alcohol makes you pee more |
| Anxiety and jitters | Rarely reported | Common ("hangxiety") |
| Sleep the night before | Often feels deep | Often broken and restless in the second half of the night |
| How long it lasts | Usually a few hours into the morning | Often most of the day, sometimes longer |
| Toxic by-product | No equivalent to acetaldehyde is known | Acetaldehyde, a toxic breakdown product of alcohol |

A few of those differences are worth explaining.

**Alcohol makes a toxic by-product. Kava doesn't make the same one.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first step produces **acetaldehyde**, a compound that's more toxic than alcohol itself and is thought to contribute to many hangover symptoms. Kava isn't broken down that way, so you don't get that piece.

**Alcohol dehydrates you more.** Alcohol lowers a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. That's why you pee so much when you drink. Kava isn't known to have that strong effect, so thirst and dehydration are usually a small part of a kava hangover. Our guide on [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers that side in more detail.

**Alcohol wrecks the second half of your sleep. Kava usually doesn't.** Alcohol often knocks you out at first and then causes a "rebound" later in the night, with lighter, broken sleep and early waking. Many kava drinkers report the opposite: a deep night's sleep, sometimes so deep it's hard to wake up. That heavy-sleep feeling is a big part of the kava hangover.

**Alcohol causes inflammation and stomach irritation. Kava is milder.** Heavy drinking irritates the stomach lining and sets off an inflammatory response that researchers think contributes to the "flu-like" side of a hangover. A big serving of kava can upset your stomach too, but usually not to the same degree.

None of this makes kava harmless. It just means the morning after tends to be milder and simpler.

## Why Kava Makes You Groggy the Next Day

Researchers are still working out exactly how kavalactones act on the brain, but a few mechanisms come up again and again in the research:

- **They calm brain activity through GABA pathways.** GABA is the brain's main "slow down" chemical messenger. Kavalactones appear to make GABA receptors more responsive, though not in the same way, or at the same site, as drugs like Xanax or Valium. That calming effect is the relaxation people go to kava for.
- **They affect the channels that let nerve cells fire.** Lab studies suggest some kavalactones dampen the sodium and calcium channels nerve cells use to send signals. In plain words, they turn down how easily nerves fire.
- **Some of the compounds linger.** The noticeable "kava feeling" usually fades within a few hours, but the compounds themselves stay in your body longer. Heavier kava, more of it, and a later session all push more of that leftover effect into the next morning.

So the grogginess isn't damage. It's mostly the tail end of the same calming effect you were looking for the night before. That's also why it's predictable: the more sedating the kava and the bigger the session, the heavier the morning.

## Noble vs Tudei Kava: The Biggest Factor You Control

If you get kava hangovers often, the variety is the first thing to check.

**Noble kava** refers to the varieties traditionally used for regular drinking. They tend to have a kavalactone mix that people describe as relaxing but clear-headed, with fewer next-day effects.

**Tudei kava** (often said to mean "two-day" in Bislama, the language of Vanuatu) has a different kavalactone mix that's heavier on the more sedating, longer-lasting compounds. The name itself comes from its reputation for effects that can last into the following day, along with more nausea. Vanuatu restricts the export of tudei kava under its national kava law for exactly this reason, though tudei and blends that include it still turn up in some products sold abroad.

What this means for you:

- **Buy from sellers who name the variety and say it's noble.** Reputable sellers usually list the cultivar and where it was grown, and many advertise testing to confirm it isn't tudei.
- **Be wary of very cheap, unlabeled, or "extra strong" kava.** These are more likely to include tudei kava or lower-quality plant parts.
- **Stick to the root.** Traditional kava uses the root and the lower part of the stem near it. The stems, leaves, and peelings have a different chemical profile and have been linked in some research to higher risk. They're not what you want in your cup.

## Kava Hangover Cure: What Actually Helps

There's no special cure, and there is no good evidence that any supplement or product "fixes" a kava hangover. The good news is you usually don't need one. These simple steps help most people feel normal faster:

1. **Eat a real breakfast.** Kava hits harder and lingers more on an empty stomach, and food helps you feel steadier. Something with protein and some carbohydrate is a good choice. Our list of [foods that help a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) has practical ideas.
2. **Drink water, but don't force gallons.** Kava isn't as dehydrating as alcohol, so a couple of normal glasses is usually plenty.
3. **Get daylight and move.** A short walk outside does a lot for that heavy, sleepy feeling. Bright light helps signal to your brain that the day has started.
4. **Have your usual coffee or tea if you normally do.** A normal amount of caffeine can take the edge off grogginess. Don't overdo it to "push through."
5. **Give it a few hours.** Most kava grogginess fades by late morning or midday. If you can, plan anything that needs sharp focus for the afternoon.
6. **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Neither more kava nor a drink will help, and mixing them is the main thing to avoid.

If you're curious about grogginess more broadly, our guide to [brain fog after drinking](/never-hungover/brain-fog-after-drinking) explains why the brain feels slow the morning after and what helps, much of which applies here too.

## How to Avoid a Kava Hangover Next Time

Prevention is easier than recovery here, because most kava hangovers come from a few predictable causes.

- **Drink less in one session.** This is the single biggest lever. If you've been drinking many shells at a bar, try fewer and see how you feel the next morning.
- **Drink earlier in the evening.** Finishing a few hours before bed gives the effect more time to wear off before you need to be awake and alert.
- **Choose noble kava.** As covered above, the variety matters a lot.
- **Prefer traditional preparations to concentrated extracts.** Water-based kava made from the root is what's been used traditionally. Concentrated extracts and high-dose products deliver more kavalactones at once and have been involved in more of the reported problems.
- **Don't drink it on a completely empty stomach,** especially if kava tends to upset your stomach. A light meal an hour or so before often helps.
- **Don't combine it with alcohol, sleep aids, or other sedatives.** Stacking sedatives is the fastest route to a much heavier morning, and it's not safe.
- **Take breaks.** Some regular, heavy kava users develop a dry, scaly skin rash called kava dermopathy, and some report more persistent sluggishness. Both are linked to heavy long-term use and generally improve when people cut back or stop.

## Kava and Alcohol Together: The Worst Kind of Hangover

This is worth its own section because it's the most common way people end up with a truly bad morning after kava.

Kava and alcohol are both depressants, and they appear to add to each other. The small amount of research on the combination has generally found more impairment when the two are taken together than with either alone. That means more sedation, more loss of coordination, and slower reactions the same night. The next morning, you don't get the "mild kava version" of a hangover. You get a full alcohol hangover with the kava grogginess layered on top.

There's also a liver angle. Both are processed by the liver, lab studies suggest kava can interfere with some of the liver enzymes that break down drugs and alcohol, and many of the rare reported cases of kava-linked liver injury involved people who were also drinking or taking other medicines. For the full picture, see our guide on [mixing kava and alcohol](/never-hungover/kava-and-alcohol).

The simple rule: pick one or the other for the night, not both. If you've had kava, leave alcohol until another day. If you've been drinking, don't use kava to "come down" or to help you sleep.

## Is a Kava Hangover a Sign of Liver Damage?

Almost always, no. A groggy morning after a kava session is the leftover calming effect, not a sign of liver injury. But kava does have a known, rare liver risk, so it's worth knowing what's normal and what isn't.

**What happened in the early 2000s.** A cluster of reports of serious liver injury in people taking kava products, mainly concentrated extracts sold in Europe, led several countries to restrict or ban kava around 2002. Germany's ban was later overturned in court, and the US FDA issued a consumer advisory about the possible liver risk rather than a ban. The World Health Organization reviewed the evidence in 2007 and concluded the risk was real but rare, and that it was likely tied to factors such as solvent-based extracts, poor-quality raw material, use of the wrong plant parts, high doses, and combination with alcohol or other drugs that strain the liver.

**What that means for you.** Traditional water-based kava from noble root, in moderate amounts, has a long history of use with few liver problems reported. The risk climbs with concentrated extracts, unknown-quality products, heavy daily use, alcohol, and existing liver problems.

**What is not normal after kava:**

- Yellow skin or yellow whites of the eyes
- Dark urine or pale, clay-colored stools
- Pain or tenderness under your right ribs
- Ongoing nausea, loss of appetite, or tiredness that doesn't lift after a day or two

If you notice any of these, stop using kava and see a doctor promptly. A simple blood test can check your liver. If you've been drinking too, our page on [liver pain after drinking](/never-hungover/liver-pain-after-drinking) explains what that discomfort may and may not mean.

## Can You Drive With a Kava Hangover?

If you still feel slow, heavy, or sleepy the next morning, don't drive. Kava impairs reaction time and coordination while it's active, and in the US, impaired-driving laws can apply to any substance that affects your driving, not just alcohol. The trouble with leftover grogginess is that it's easy to underestimate. You may feel "mostly fine" while your reactions are still a step behind.

A practical rule: if you'd hesitate to say you feel fully alert, wait. A breakfast, some daylight, and an hour or two usually make the difference. And never drive the same night as a kava session, especially if any alcohol was involved.

## Kava vs Kratom: Not the Same Thing

Many kava bars also sell kratom, and people sometimes lump the two together. They are very different.

**Kava** is a calming root drink from the Pacific that acts mainly through GABA-related pathways. **Kratom** comes from the leaves of a Southeast Asian tree (*Mitragyna speciosa*) and acts partly on the same receptors as opioid drugs. Kratom's morning-after effects, side effects, and risks are different, and it can cause dependence and withdrawal with regular use. The FDA has warned consumers about kratom's safety.

If you felt unusually rough after a night at a kava bar, it's worth asking yourself whether you only had kava, or whether kratom or a mixed drink was part of the evening. Everything in this guide applies to kava only.

## Kava as an Alternative to a Night of Drinking

A lot of people try kava because they want to relax socially without the alcohol hangover. That's a fair reason, and for a healthy adult, a moderate amount of good-quality noble kava is likely to leave you feeling better the next day than a night of heavy drinking would. If you're cutting back on alcohol and want ideas for replacing the ritual, our guide to being [sober curious](/never-hungover/sober-curious) covers that.

A few honest caveats:

- **It still impairs you.** Kava isn't a "free" substitute. Don't drive on it.
- **The calming research is mixed.** Some older reviews of kava extract for anxiety found it worked better than placebo, while a larger, longer trial from Australian researchers published in 2020 did not find a clear benefit over placebo for generalized anxiety. It may help some people relax, but it's not a proven treatment.
- **It doesn't treat alcohol cravings or withdrawal.** There is no good evidence that kava helps with that. If you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you skip drinking, talk to a doctor, because alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous and there are effective treatments.
- **It interacts with medicines.** Anyone on prescription medication, especially for mood, anxiety, sleep, pain, or seizures, should ask a pharmacist before using kava.

## Who Should Be Most Careful With Kava

You're more likely to have a rough morning, or a more serious problem, if you:

- Have **liver disease** or have been told your liver enzymes are high
- **Drink alcohol** regularly, or plan to drink the same day
- Take **sedating medicines** such as benzodiazepines, sleep aids, opioid pain medicines, some antidepressants, or seizure medicines
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding** (kava isn't recommended)
- Use **concentrated extracts** or products where the variety and plant part aren't listed
- Drink kava **heavily every day**

If any of these describe you, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using kava. They can look at your full medication list.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

To be clear about this, **DHM is not a kava hangover remedy.** DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that has been studied for its effects on *alcohol* metabolism and on GABA receptors in the context of alcohol. There is no research on DHM for kava, and no reason to expect it to help with kava grogginess. It also doesn't make it safe to mix kava and alcohol.

Where DHM may be relevant is on the nights you choose alcohol instead. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that any supplement prevents hangovers outright. If you want to try it on drinking nights, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter far more than any pill: pacing, food, water, and sleep.

## The Bottom Line

- A kava hangover is real but usually mild: grogginess, heaviness, slow thinking, and sometimes a little nausea, mostly gone by late morning.
- It feels different from an alcohol hangover because kava doesn't produce acetaldehyde, isn't strongly dehydrating, and tends to deepen sleep rather than break it up.
- The biggest causes are a large session, tudei or poor-quality kava, an empty stomach, and mixing with alcohol.
- Food, water, daylight, a normal coffee, and a few hours are usually all you need. Don't drive while you still feel slow.
- Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pain under the right ribs, or lingering nausea and fatigue are not a normal kava hangover. Stop using kava and see a doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does kava give you a hangover?**

It can. After a large session or strong kava, many people wake up groggy, heavy, and slow for a few hours. After a moderate amount of good-quality noble kava, many people feel normal. A kava hangover is usually much milder than an alcohol hangover and rarely includes a bad headache, heavy nausea, or anxiety.

**What does a kava hangover feel like?**

Most people describe sleepiness and heaviness, slow thinking, and low motivation, sometimes with mild nausea or tired eyes. It's more like leftover sedation than the headache-and-nausea hangover alcohol causes. It usually fades by late morning or midday, faster once you eat and move around.

**How long does a kava hangover last?**

Usually a few hours into the next morning. Heavier sessions, stronger or tudei kava, and drinking late in the evening can stretch it into the afternoon. If you still feel unwell after a day or two, or you notice yellow skin, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs, see a doctor.

**What is the best kava hangover cure?**

There's no special cure, and there is no good evidence any supplement fixes it. Eat a proper breakfast, drink a couple of glasses of water, get some daylight and a short walk, and have your usual coffee or tea. Most people feel normal within a few hours. Don't use more kava or alcohol to feel better.

**Is a kava hangover worse than an alcohol hangover?**

Usually not. Kava doesn't produce acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol, and it isn't strongly dehydrating, so the morning after is typically milder. The exception is when you mix kava with alcohol: then you get the full alcohol hangover plus kava grogginess on top.

**Why does tudei kava cause a worse hangover?**

Tudei kava has a different mix of kavalactones that leans toward the more sedating, longer-lasting compounds, which is where its "two-day" name comes from. It's also more often linked to nausea. Vanuatu restricts its export for this reason. Choosing noble kava from a seller who names the variety is the easiest way to avoid it.

**Is it safe to drive after drinking kava the night before?**

Only if you feel fully alert. Kava impairs reaction time and coordination while it's active, and leftover grogginess is easy to underestimate. If you still feel slow or sleepy, wait until it lifts. Never drive the same night as a kava session.

**Can a kava hangover mean liver damage?**

Almost always no. Normal grogginess is leftover sedation, not liver injury. But kava has a rare, real liver risk, mostly linked to concentrated extracts, poor-quality products, heavy use, and alcohol. Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, pain under the right ribs, or lasting nausea and fatigue are not normal, so stop using kava and see a doctor.

**Does DHM help with a kava hangover?**

There is no research on DHM for kava, and no reason to expect it to help with kava grogginess. DHM has been studied for alcohol, mostly in animal and lab research, and it doesn't make mixing kava and alcohol safe.
